text: She was reading the clause when the phone rang.
While the lawyers were arguing, the broker was asking the port.
We were finishing due diligence when the regulator called.
Nobody was moving, and nobody was calling anybody.
We were finishing due diligence when the regulator asked for a document.
The deal closed eleven days late, and nobody backed out.
We were finalizing the contract when the broker called.
Tell me what was happening when it stopped.
It was almost midnight and nobody was going home.

I want to tell you about the worst hour of my career, because everybody remembers the decision and nobody remembers the hour before it. We were finalizing a contract at eleven at night. My associate was checking the numbers, the client was waiting on the other line, and I was reading the delivery clause for the third time. Then the broker called and the ship turned around. Here is what I learned that night. When something interrupts a negotiation, the first question is never who is right. The first question is: what exactly was happening at that moment, and who can prove it? While we were arguing about the cause, somebody with no law degree was asking the port for a document, and that document decided everything. The lesson is not humility. The lesson is that a fact beats an argument, and a fact is usually somewhere nobody is looking.

People imagine that big deals collapse because somebody says no. In my experience they collapse because nothing happens. I was advising a client during a long acquisition, and the two sides had already agreed on the price. We were finishing due diligence, the lawyers were writing the last version, and everybody was expecting a signature before Christmas. Then the regulator asked for one more document, and nobody sent it, because each side thought the other one was sending it. Six weeks later the buyer backed out. Nobody argued. Nobody sent an angry email. The deal simply stopped moving while everybody was waiting for somebody else. That is what a deadlock actually looks like from the inside, and it almost never looks like a fight.

We were finalizing the contract when the broker called.
While the lawyers were arguing, the broker was asking the port.
What were you doing when the client called?
Nobody knew what caused the delay.

It was almost midnight and nobody was going home.
